subject: mechanical
audience: FE Mechanical candidates and mechanical engineering students
title: The 50 m Pipe That Lost 20 kPa
featured_title: THE 50 M PIPE THAT LOST 20 KPA

presentation.challenge: The velocity stayed at 2 m/s, yet wall friction consumed 20 kPa of pressure over the pipe length.

practice.primary_question: How does the Darcy-Weisbach equation convert pipe friction into pressure drop?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Using only dynamic pressure and forgetting the dimensionless length-to-diameter multiplier in Darcy-Weisbach loss.

case_dna.target_misconception: A constant-diameter pipe with constant flow speed should have no pressure loss because velocity does not change.
case_dna.why_plausible: Bernoulli's ideal form can make constant elevation and constant velocity look like constant pressure.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: Wall friction causes irreversible loss. For f=0.02, L=50 m, D=0.10 m, ρ=1000 kg/m³, and V=2 m/s, ΔP=f(L/D)(ρV²/2)=20 kPa.
case_dna.corrected_model: Real internal flow requires a friction-loss term. Darcy-Weisbach scales loss with f, L/D, and dynamic pressure.

problem_statement: Water flows at 2.0 m/s through a 50 m long, 0.10 m diameter horizontal pipe. Use a Darcy friction factor f=0.020 and density 1000 kg/m³. A review predicts no pressure drop because pipe diameter, velocity, and elevation are constant. Calculate the frictional pressure loss.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: Velocity stayed constant. Static pressure still fell.
gates.prompt: What real-flow term is missing from an ideal constant-velocity Bernoulli argument?

gates.label: Theory
gates.heading: Choose the correct internal-flow loss model

options.label: Set ΔP=0 because velocity and elevation are constant
Use only ρV²/2 as the pressure loss
options.reason: Dynamic pressure is multiplied by fL/D for the Darcy friction loss.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the pressure drop
gates.prompt: What frictional pressure drop in kPa occurs over the 50 m pipe?

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Measure pressure along the line
gates.result: The pressure drops by about 20 kPa.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: Friction consumes mechanical energy even without acceleration

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the pipe-pressure note
report: C2. Diameter and velocity are constant.
C3. Therefore the pressure cannot decrease.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: It ignores frictional energy loss along the wall.

evidence_choices.label: Darcy-Weisbach gives ΔP=20 kPa
evidence_choices.reason: This quantifies the distributed friction loss.

correction.template: The 50 m pipe loses about {drop} kPa to wall friction.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Cut the Darcy pressure drop in half
gates.constraint: Keep f, D, and V unchanged.

options.label: Reduce pipe length from 50 m to 25 m
options.reason: Darcy loss is directly proportional to L.

options.label: Keep the same pipe but omit the friction term
options.reason: That changes the model, not the physical loss.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply Darcy-Weisbach scaling
gates.prompt: If velocity doubles while f, L, D, and density remain fixed, how does Darcy pressure loss change?
gates.explanation: With other terms fixed, Darcy-Weisbach pressure loss scales with velocity squared.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the pipe-loss model
gates.confirmation: I confirm that real constant-diameter pipe flow can lose pressure because of wall friction even when velocity and elevation are unchanged.

items.label: What failed
items.value: An ideal-flow argument predicted zero pressure loss.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Use Darcy-Weisbach loss with fL/D and dynamic pressure.

seo.seo_title: Darcy-Weisbach Pressure Drop: Why a 50 m Pipe Loses 20 kPa | FE E-055
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Mechanical Case E-055: water at 2 m/s in a 50 m, 0.10 m pipe with f=0.02 loses 20 kPa by Darcy-Weisbach friction.
seo.focus_keyphrase: FE Mechanical Darcy Weisbach pressure drop
seo.excerpt: Constant velocity does not mean constant pressure in real pipe flow. Wall friction causes distributed energy loss.
seo.direct_answer: Darcy-Weisbach gives ΔP=f(L/D)(ρV²/2). With f=0.02, L=50 m, D=0.10 m, ρ=1000 kg/m³, and V=2 m/s, the pressure loss is 20,000 Pa, or 20 kPa.

faqs.q: Can pressure fall in a constant-diameter horizontal pipe?
faqs.a: Yes. Wall friction causes pressure loss even when average velocity and elevation are unchanged.

faqs.q: How does Darcy pressure loss scale with velocity?
faqs.a: Approximately with V² when the other terms, including friction factor, are held fixed.
